title: The Multiplier Effect
hook: A wrong edition teaches the wrong source. Everyone agreed, but no one knew who would bring back proof.
counterintuition: The small source line is not clerical. It decides which lesson you are allowed to teach and which proof you still owe.
tryThisNow: When you cite a source today, circle the edition marker and one fact it permits before you use the claim.
keyTakeaway: Anchor the source before the lesson: circle the edition marker, separate the 2017 revision from 2010 records, then judge the effect by behavior around people.

breakdown.fastRead:
A wrong edition teaches the wrong source. Everyone agreed, but no one knew who would bring back proof.

Harvard Business Review (a May 2010 management article venue) gives the early mark: Liz Wiseman and Greg McKeown had already made the Diminisher and Multiplier contrast public. The publisher record for Multipliers gives a later mark: May 16, 2017 is the revised listing.

Mark the source line first. A May 16, 2017 line puts you in the revised edition. If the line says June 15, 2010, you are holding the original record. The wrong record makes a true idea point at the wrong source.
breakdown.deepRead:
Edition comes first because it decides what the claim is allowed to carry. A source can be true and still be the wrong source for the sentence you wrote.

In May 2010, Harvard Business Review carried both named authors under the same article. The article framed two kinds of conduct: Diminishers drain others' intelligence, while Multipliers draw it out. That is not a manners scale. It asks whether people around the person in charge give more judgment, challenge, and follow-through.

Now put that beside the publisher listing. The revised listing carries May 16, 2017 and names 150-plus leaders as its base, plus five disciplines. Those details do different jobs. The HBR article proves the contrast was already public; the 2017 record tells you when the revised source begins. Both can be true. They do not do the same job.

Circle the edition before you teach the claim. The date written where the group reads it can save the idea from the wrong source. Without it, a reader may use the first-release record to defend added revised material, or use the 2017 listing as if it created the whole distinction.

The human part is just as sharp. A Diminisher can be smart and still leave less usable judgment behind. The smartest answer in the room can be the reason the room gets less smart. Who gets smaller after you speak? Watch that evidence, not the self-image.
breakdown.fullRead:
Start with the record that can pay for the sentence. If you teach the revised Multipliers source, the publisher listing with May 16, 2017 has to stand under that sentence. If you teach only the first release, the June 15, 2010 publisher record does a different job.

That sounds like a library chore. It is not. Edition drift is how a careful person makes a false bridge: the idea is real, the source is real, and the join between them is weak. Once the join weakens, the reader cannot tell which added material was actually in view.

The HBR article gives the cleanest guardrail. May 2010 comes before the 2017 revision, and the two named authors are on that public article. So the contrast between Diminisher and Multiplier is not a late invention. A Diminisher drains usable intelligence by making other minds less needed. A Multiplier raises the amount of judgment people bring after contact with that person.

The publisher adds the second guardrail. The revised edition record names the on-sale marker, the data from more than 150 leaders, and five disciplines. Use that record when the claim needs the revised source. Do not ask the 2010 original record to prove what belongs to 2017. A clean number can still point to the wrong shelf.

This is why the productivity claim matters. The promise is not "be nicer and people will feel good." It is doing more with fewer resources by using intelligence already near you. If that sounds soft, look at the evidence you can see after you speak: more thought, more owned effort, more useful challenge. If the answer still comes from one person and others wait, the label did not do much.

You can run the same move without a title. When you cite a file, a training note, or an old record, ask who owes whom what by when. The artifact must tell the same story as the claim. If the source line says 2010, let it prove the 2010 contrast. If the source line says May 16, 2017, let it carry the revised frame. Put the edition mark in place before the lesson starts.

Had they not kept those records apart, three mistakes would follow. The revised edition would look like the birthplace of the Diminisher and Multiplier contrast. The 2010 original record would look strong enough to prove the revised contents. And the research base of more than 150 leaders would shrink in the reader's mind into one good executive tale.

The reversal is simple. You are not checking a source after the lesson; you are checking the source so the lesson has a right to stand. That habit protects the bigger idea. Multiplying is not self-praise. It is the observable change in how others think, decide, and carry effort after dealing with you.

Use the move where the source boundary affects the claim. It does not belong on every low-stakes note, and it can slow a fast handoff. If no added material or version gap is at stake, name the idea and move. If the record will decide what is included, do the opposite: slow down, circle the edition, and keep the marked source line tied to the right source.

examples.title: The Earlier Issue

planSpec.stakes: later material rides on an early article
planSpec.requiredBeat: spot the early signal before revised claims attach

examples.scenario: A source analyst sees May 2010 as the early signal, but it can hide in plain sight. Liz Wiseman and Greg McKeown already appear under the Harvard Business Review article, on a page that predates the revised listing. The consequence is open: the article proves the contrast is public, but it cannot yet tell which 2017 additions belong to the revised source.
examples.whatToDo: Keep the early mark narrow. Use the HBR article for the public contrast, then require a separate 2017 line for any revised claim.
examples.whyItMatters: Miss this and a true early article starts carrying later material. You protect the contrast by naming what the May 2010 article can and cannot prove.

examples.title: The Revised Standard

planSpec.stakes: revised material is tied to the wrong record
planSpec.requiredBeat: state the revised standard before source mixing begins

examples.scenario: The Multipliers revised listing states the standard: May 16, 2017, more than 150 leaders, five disciplines. That demand costs something. The 2010 record cannot prove revised material, so the easier old identifier loses the job and the 2017 publisher record carries the claim.
examples.whatToDo: Skip the standard and the old identifier will do work it cannot do. Put the May 16, 2017 line beside the revised claim before you cite the broader data.
examples.whyItMatters: Leave the cost unpaid and the revised edition turns into a blur. The hard source line lets the reader know which material is in view.

examples.title: The Original Catch

planSpec.stakes: original release is made to prove later contents
planSpec.requiredBeat: catch the original-release record after it has been overused

examples.scenario: A trainer is already pasting the 2010 record into the revised claim. Too late, the Harpercollins catalog finding stops it: the Multipliers original release belongs to June 15, 2010, not to the revised material. Had they not caught that line, the first record would have been made to prove later contents. The miss is barely avoided.
examples.whatToDo: It works because the number has one job. Move the 2010 marker back to the original release, then use the 2017 listing for revised material.
examples.whyItMatters: A late catch still matters. The original record can separate the first source, but it cannot pay for claims added to the later one.

examples.title: The Partial Answer

planSpec.stakes: early proof is asked to settle later material
planSpec.requiredBeat: name what the early article proves and what stays open

examples.scenario: At the pass, a source analyst asks what the early article can settle. The May 2010 Harvard Business Review article answers one thing: Liz Wiseman and Greg McKeown had already made the Diminisher and Multiplier contrast public. The move half-works because the article does not settle which revised material came later.
examples.whatToDo: Does the early article settle the revised source? No. Let it prove the contrast, then send added claims back to the May 16, 2017 listing.
examples.whyItMatters: This keeps the win partial. You avoid the false invention claim, but you still need the revised record for what changed after 2010.

examples.title: The Larger Base

planSpec.stakes: a broad base shrinks into one story
planSpec.requiredBeat: trace the single-story miss back to the source number

examples.scenario: After the source pass, one draft line explains why the single-story version failed: more than 150 leaders. Multipliers ties that scale to the revised listing with May 16, 2017 and five disciplines. The single executive tale loses its lead, and the research base becomes the ground for the claim.
examples.whatToDo: Cut the lone tale before it becomes proof. Let the more than 150 leaders carry the claim, with the May 16, 2017 record beside it.
examples.whyItMatters: One story shrinks the base. The revised listing makes the claim broader, and the cost is that a memorable tale cannot do all the teaching.

examples.title: The Downstream Mix

planSpec.stakes: a reader learns the wrong source boundary
planSpec.requiredBeat: show the downstream effect before the source mix is corrected

examples.scenario: A partner downstream first feels the effect when revised material is taught with only the original release attached. The match looks close enough until the Harpercollins catalog finding points back to June 15, 2010 and Multipliers. The miss is caught late, barely, and the claim changes before the reader learns the wrong source boundary.
examples.whatToDo: Stop the wrong boundary before it travels. Pair the original release with original content, then require the revised listing for revised claims.
examples.whyItMatters: Let it travel and the reader pays with confusion. The source boundary is part of the lesson, not a cleanup task after the lesson.

questions.prompt: Your reading group has two Multipliers records open while preparing a handout, and the handout will teach revised material. Which source move comes first?
choices: Use the older identifier if it is easier for the reading group to find.
Start with the May 16, 2017 publisher listing before teaching revised content.
Treat both records as the same since the reading group is teaching one title for this handout.
questions.explanation: The revised listing sets which content belongs to that source. The older-identifier choice is tempting, but it points to the original record and cannot settle revised material.

questions.prompt: When a department is short on staff, a director says Multipliers is mainly about happier employees. What consequence should you predict?
choices: The department may add a comfort program while leaving paid-for capability unused.
The department misses the operating claim: get more output from intelligence already nearby.
The department should ask for headcount first because capability cannot rise inside the current group.
questions.explanation: The model is not only a mood claim. It says unused capability is a resource. The comfort-program answer starts near engagement but stops before output.

questions.prompt: A supervisor stays kind during a budget call but makes every important decision alone before anyone can add judgment. Which principle does that break?
choices: The contrast turns on whether others' judgment is used, not whether the supervisor sounds warm.
The contrast is mostly about whether the supervisor avoids harsh language during tense choices.
The supervisor can count as a Multiplier if the final calls spare others from pressure.
questions.explanation: Kindness is not the test. The key issue is usable intelligence around the person in charge. The warm-language choice mistakes tone for contribution.

questions.prompt: Training notes cite the 2010 original identifier to support a claim about the revised edition. What is the best correction?
choices: Keep the identifier if the training notes also mention that the publisher released the title.
Drop the bibliographic line because source records distract from the leadership idea.
Use the identifier only for the June 15, 2010 original, not as proof of revised contents.
questions.explanation: That identifier marks the original release. It is useful, but not for revised additions. The publisher mention alone does not change which edition it identifies.

questions.prompt: A consultant builds the whole lesson from one memorable executive tale. What should change before the lesson is trusted?
choices: Tie the claim to the revised edition's data from more than 150 leaders.
Keep the executive tale central because one clear story is easier to remember.
Use the publication year alone, since a date proves the research scale.
questions.explanation: The source base is broader than one profile. A single tale may help explain, but it cannot replace the 150-plus-leader base named in the listing.

questions.prompt: During a product call, the smartest person supplies every answer while engineers who know the edge cases stop weighing in. What explains the drop?
choices: The product call needs a sharper expert, since stronger answers raise total intelligence.
One person's brilliance has crowded out judgment that should be coming from others.
The product call should keep decisions with the expert until others feel more ready.
questions.explanation: High intelligence in one person can still lower the total intelligence in use. The sharper-expert answer repeats the error in the product call.

questions.prompt: After a director calls herself empowering during a project reset, the staff still waits for her to make each decision. Which evidence matters most?
choices: Her self-description matters if the staff believes she means it.
Her intent matters more than the staff's behavior after each exchange.
Whether people think harder and own more after interacting with her.
questions.explanation: Self-image is not the measure. The observable effect around her is. The intent answer sounds fair, but it leaves the staff's waiting untouched.

questions.prompt: Someone says they cannot use the Multiplier idea because they are not naturally charismatic. What is the single best reply?
choices: Work on the five disciplines as learnable practices instead of waiting for a new personality.
Use the idea only if charisma is already one of the person's strongest traits in public settings.
Begin with a public confidence boost so the five disciplines feel easier to try.
questions.explanation: The disciplines are framed as learnable. The charisma answer narrows the model to a gift, while the confidence-boost answer changes mood before routine.

questions.prompt: An internal newsletter says the 2017 revision invented the Diminisher and Multiplier distinction. What is the best fix?
choices: Use the original record alone, since it can prove every part of the contrast.
Leave the newsletter as written if it links to the revised publisher listing.
Point to the May 2010 HBR article by Liz Wiseman and Greg McKeown.
questions.explanation: The public article predates the revision and carries both names. The revised listing matters, but it cannot be treated as the origin of the distinction.

reviewCards.front: What should you circle before using a source claim?
reviewCards.back: Circle the edition marker first. The May 16, 2017 publisher listing separates revised material from the 2010 original record.

reviewCards.front: How can the smartest answer reduce the total intelligence in use?
reviewCards.back: When one person centers every answer, others stop adding judgment. The result can be less usable intelligence, even if that one answer is sharp.

reviewCards.front: Why does the more than 150 leaders detail matter?
reviewCards.back: It keeps the framework from shrinking into one executive story. The revised edition presents a broader research base, so a single tale cannot carry the proof.

reviewCards.front: What evidence beats a person's empowering self-image?
reviewCards.back: Look at what happens around that person. If others think harder and own more after the exchange, the effect is visible; the self-label alone is not enough.

reviewCards.front: When does the June 15, 2010 original record help, and when does it fail?
reviewCards.back: It helps identify the first release. It fails when used to prove revised material tied to the 2017 listing.

reviewCards.front: How do learnable disciplines change the reader's action?
reviewCards.back: They move the idea away from natural charisma. You can change routines and practice the five disciplines instead of waiting to become a different kind of person.

implementationPlan.title: Circle the Edition
implementationPlan.coreSkill: Circle the Edition. Before you teach a claim, mark the source line that tells you which version you are using. Then name what that line can prove and what it cannot carry.

ifThenPlans.plan: If a claim uses revised material, then circle May 16, 2017 before you cite it.
If the 2010 original identifier appears, then keep it with the June 15, 2010 original.
If someone claims to multiply others, then look for harder thought and more owned effort around them.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Teach the move to one person in 5 minutes: circle the edition marker on one source line, explain what the mark includes, and ask them to restate it.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Each week, count one number: live claims with an edition marker circled before use. Raise the count by one before you add a new source.

memorableLines.text: Who gets smaller after you speak?
memorableLines.why: It turns the effect into a question the reader can use after any exchange.

memorableLines.text: Circle the edition before you teach the claim.
memorableLines.why: It gives the source move in a short command.

memorableLines.text: The smartest answer in the room can be the reason the room gets less smart.
memorableLines.why: It reverses the usual faith in individual brilliance.
